whisper_prompt: Mathematics. Geometry. Sphere. Great circle. Geodesic. Latitude. Longitude. Euclidean.

sections.title: A QUESTION ABOUT THE SHORTEST WALK
animations: Compare routes on a flat sheet
Introduce a tiny ant and two endpoints
sections.narration: Imagine a tiny ant standing at one point and trying to reach another. On a flat sheet, the answer feels obvious: draw a straight line. In ordinary Euclidean geometry, a straight segment is the shortest route between two points. But now place the ant on a sphere. The ant cannot tunnel through the middle. It must stay on the surface. Does straight still mean shortest?

sections.title: STRAIGHT THROUGH OR CURVED AROUND
animations: Show a chord through a sphere
Show a surface route following the sphere
sections.narration: There are two different questions hiding here. The straight chord through the sphere is shorter in three dimensional space, but it leaves the surface immediately. The ant is constrained to the outside, so that chord is not an allowed path. We are measuring distance inside the surface, not distance through the solid. The constraint changes the geometry.

sections.title: THE GREAT CIRCLE
animations: Rotate a plane through two points
Reveal the great-circle arc and move the ant
sections.narration: Take the two points and the center of the sphere. Exactly one plane passes through all three, unless the points are opposite each other. Where that plane cuts the sphere, it creates a great circle. Its center is the sphere's center, so the circle has the largest possible radius. The shorter arc between the points is the surface's straightest route: a geodesic.

sections.title: WHY LATITUDE LINES FOOL US
animations: Show the latitude route is longer than the geodesic
sections.narration: The equator is a great circle. But most latitude lines are smaller circles, because their centers sit above or below the sphere's center. They look straight on a familiar map, yet they are not the shortest surface routes between their points. The sphere is quietly changing the meaning of a straight line beneath the map.

sections.title: THE MAP IS THE DISTORTION
animations: Unwrap a globe into a rectangular map
Compare a straight map line with a great-circle curve
sections.narration: Flatten the globe into a rectangular map and the great-circle path often becomes a curve. That curve is not taking a detour. The map is distorting the surface to make it flat. A route that looks straight on a map can be longer on the planet, while the curved route records the true shortest path on the sphere.

sections.title: THE RULE IN ONE EQUATION
animations: Let the ant finish on the great-circle arc
sections.narration: For a sphere of radius R, with central angle theta in radians, the great-circle distance is R times theta. The ant has discovered a different kind of straightness. In flat space, straight lines minimize distance. On a curved surface, geodesics do. The shortest path is the straightest path the surface allows.
